statement:
Given an array `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, merge every group of overlapping intervals and return the list of non-overlapping intervals that together cover exactly the same points.

Intervals that share an endpoint, such as `[1,4]` and `[4,5]`, are considered overlapping. Return the merged intervals **sorted by start**.

examples.explanation: They touch at `4`, so they merge.
The input need not be sorted.

hints: Overlapping intervals are easy to spot once intervals with nearby starts sit next to each other.
Sort by start, then sweep once while keeping the last interval of the output as the one you are currently growing.
For each interval, if its start is `<=` the last output interval's end, extend that end to `max(end, current end)`; otherwise append it as a new interval.

why.d: Checks intervals that are all identical.

variants.title: Total covered length
variants.approach: Sort, merge on the fly, sum merged lengths · O(n log n) time
variants.statement:
Each `intervals[i] = [start, end]` is a segment on the number line with length `end - start`. Segments may overlap and are unsorted.

Return the **total length covered by at least one segment** (overlapping parts count once).

examples.explanation: They touch at 4 and together cover [1,5]: length 4.

hints: Overlaps are easy to see once intervals are sorted by start.
Merge as you go, keeping only the current merged block.
When a new interval starts after the block ends, add the block length and start a new one.

why.d: Checks a 1×2 strip and an input whose answer is 0.
Checks a 1×2 strip and an input whose answer is 0.

solutions.name: Elementary Segments
solutions.description: Sort all distinct endpoints; each gap between consecutive endpoints is either fully covered or fully uncovered. Add a gap's length whenever some segment contains it.

solutions.name: Sort, Merge on the Fly, Sum Merged Lengths (Optimal)
solutions.description: Sort by start and sweep, keeping the current merged block [start, end]. An interval starting after end closes the block (add its length); otherwise it just extends end.

variants.title: Merge adjacent ranges
variants.approach: Sort, merge when next start ≤ end + 1 · O(n log n) time
variants.statement:
Each `intervals[i] = [a, b]` stands for the **set of integers** `a, a+1, …, b`. Merge them so that the result describes the same integers with as few ranges as possible — ranges that overlap **or are adjacent** (like `[1,2]` and `[3,5]`) must be combined.

Return the merged ranges sorted by start.

examples.explanation: [1,2] and [3,5] have no integer gap between them, giving [[1,5],[8,9]].
5 is missing, so they stay separate.

hints: This is the classic merge with a relaxed overlap test.
Extend the last merged range when `a ≤ last_end + 1`; otherwise start a new one.

solutions.name: Brute Force (Repeated Pair Merging)
solutions.description: Keep scanning for any two ranges that overlap or sit next to each other (one starts at most one past the other's end), replace them with their union, and repeat until no pair merges. Sort what is left.
keyPoints: Mergeable if a₂ ≤ b₁ + 1 and a₁ ≤ b₂ + 1

solutions.name: Sort, Merge When Next Start ≤ End + 1 (Optimal)
solutions.description: Sort by start and sweep: a range joins the last merged range when it starts no later than one past that range's end (overlapping or integer-adjacent); otherwise it opens a new range.

solutions.name: Brute Force (Compare All Pairs)
solutions.description: Compare every pair of intervals and merge overlapping ones iteratively.
keyPoints: Merge if current start <= previous end
This is already the optimal approach

solutions.name: Sort and Merge (Optimal)
solutions.description: Sort intervals by start time, then iterate and merge overlapping intervals into the result.
keyPoints: Update end of last merged interval
